title: Turnkey vs. Traditional: A Guide for Luxury Homeowners
excerpt: One contract, one accountable team, one vision — here's how a turnkey approach compares to managing architects, contractors and designers separately.
content:
Building or renovating a luxury home traditionally means assembling your own team: an architect, an interior designer, a structural engineer, a contractor, and someone to manage all of them. A turnkey model replaces that with a single accountable studio. Here's how the two actually compare.

Accountability

In a traditional model, when something goes wrong, the architect blames the contractor, the contractor blames the timeline, and the homeowner is left mediating. In a turnkey model, one team owns the outcome end to end — design, procurement, execution and handover.

Timeline

Traditional projects lose weeks, sometimes months, to handoffs between disconnected teams who were never in the same room during design. A turnkey studio designs with construction sequencing in mind from day one, which is where most real time savings come from.

"The biggest cost overruns we've seen in traditional projects didn't come from materials — they came from miscommunication between teams that never should have existed in the first place."

Cost Predictability

  • Traditional: multiple contracts, multiple change-order processes, multiple points of price escalation
  • Turnkey: a single scope, priced and locked before execution begins

When Traditional Still Makes Sense

For heritage restorations requiring highly specialised conservation architects, or for clients who genuinely want to hand-pick every specialist themselves, a traditional model can still be the right call. It simply asks more of the homeowner as project manager.

Our Recommendation

For most luxury homeowners balancing demanding schedules against exacting standards, turnkey removes the coordination burden without removing creative control — because the same studio designing the space is the one building it.
